title: Confessions of a Middle Manager
author: Gaurav Jain
summary: Drawing on two decades in corporate management, Gaurav Jain presents middle management as a misunderstood and paradoxical role, the bridge between strategy and execution. The piece is organized as nine first-person 'confessions', each built around a concrete episode: an impossible deadline, an upbeat all-hands delivered ahead of a known restructuring, powerlessness during reorganizations, hard feedback to a brilliant but abrasive engineer, imposter syndrome, being caught between two senior leaders, quietly bending a rigid leave policy, enforcing unpopular policies, and small coping indulgences. Each confession ends with practical takeaways, such as never committing to a project without the team, not passing the buck on decisions, and pushing for policy change rather than repeated workarounds. The argument is that these tensions are the normal human texture of management, not signs of weakness.
points: Middle managers are held accountable for results while having little authority over the big levers, so they should focus on what they can control: morale, communication and execution.

Delivering messages one does not fully believe in forces a choice between loyalty upward and trust downward; the author advises seeking deeper context and being pragmatic rather than falsely enthusiastic.
Hard feedback is framed as part of the job because leadership 'isn't about being liked' but about being fair, direct and invested in growth.
The author defends discreetly bending a rigid policy for a deserving employee while urging managers to push for policy change if they keep making the same exception.
When enforcing unpopular decisions, saying 'I don't agree with this either' damages the manager's integrity more than it builds trust; providing context works better.
quotes: For more than two decades, I’ve navigated the trenches of the corporate workplace—sometimes as a front-line manager, other times as the leader of large, matrixed teams spread across geographies. I’ve reported to over 15 different managers, often juggling multiple reporting lines at once. I’ve been at the center of strategy discussions while also managing the day-to-day chaos of execution.

It’s a tightrope walk, one where you constantly have to translate strategy into execution while keeping your team motivated. When you’re squeezed from both sides, it’s easy to feel like you’re failing someone, no matter what you do.

Every middle manager has faced this dilemma—having to sell an idea they don’t fully believe in. The challenge is walking the fine line between loyalty to leadership and maintaining trust with your team. While I try to be as authentic as possible, there are times when I’ve had to play the role of the enthusiastic messenger, even when my gut said otherwise.

Middle managers are expected to lead, but in reality, we often have limited control over major decisions. We are held accountable for results, yet have little authority over the big levers that shape our work. It’s one of the most frustrating parts of the job—feeling like a decision-maker while realizing you’re mostly an executor.

Giving tough feedback is an inevitable part of management, something middle managers need to embrace as a regular part of their job. It’s never easy, especially when you know it could hurt someone’s confidence. But leadership isn’t about being liked—it’s about being fair, direct, and invested in people’s growth.
Sometimes, being a good manager means bending rules that don’t make sense. It’s a fine line between discretion and bending rules, but at the end of the day, leadership is about people, not policies.

Being a middle manager means owning decisions you don’t always agree with. It’s an uncomfortable position—we act as the face of decisions made at a higher level, even when we have little or no say in them. Employees expect us to advocate for them, yet leadership expects us to execute.
